quiz.question: What does eventual consistency generally guarantee?
options: Every read immediately sees the latest global write
Replicas eventually converge if updates stop and synchronization succeeds under the model's assumptions
All concurrent writes are rejected
quiz.explanation: Eventual consistency ensures that in the absence of new mutations, all replicas will eventually synchronize and return identical data. It does not provide a hard real-time upper bound on propagation delay.

quiz.question: What is the defining real-time property of linearizability?
options: Operations appear atomic in an order that respects real-time precedence for non-overlapping operations
Every write must reach every physical server before returning
Every operation has a globally synchronized wall-clock timestamp
quiz.explanation: Linearizability requires that if operation A completes before operation B begins in absolute physical time, B must observe A's completed state (or a subsequent state). Operations appear to execute instantaneously on a single logical object.

quiz.question: For N=3, R=2, W=2, what is the minimum size of the intersection between any read and write quorums in the simple fixed-replica-set model?
quiz.explanation: By the pigeonhole formula: min_intersection = max(0, R + W - N) = max(0, 2 + 2 - 3) = 1. Every read quorum shares at least 1 node with every write quorum.

quiz.question: What does R + W > N establish in the simplified quorum model?
options: It proves complete linearizability for any database
It guarantees that every read quorum intersects every write quorum for the same fixed replica set
It guarantees that no replica can fail
quiz.explanation: The condition R + W > N guarantees mathematical set intersection between the read and write replicas. However, achieving linearizability still requires correct version selection, conflict resolution, and synchronization protocols.

quiz.question: What is read-your-writes consistency?
options: A client can observe its own completed write in subsequent reads under the guarantee
Every read must be executed on the same physical server
Every replica must be updated simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Read-your-writes guarantees that whenever an individual client commits a mutation, all subsequent reads executed by that same client within its session will reflect that mutation.

quiz.question: A quorum write succeeds while one replica remains stale. What may help the replicas converge?
options: Read repair or background anti-entropy repair
Changing all application timestamps to local time
Disabling every read request
quiz.explanation: Read repair updates stale replicas when an inconsistent read is detected, while background anti-entropy repair (such as Cassandra Merkle tree synchronization) periodically compares and synchronizes drifted data.

quiz.question: What is a major risk of last-write-wins conflict resolution?
options: It always rejects concurrent writes
The selected value may be undesirable if timestamp order does not reflect the intended business decision
It makes quorum intersection impossible
quiz.explanation: Last-Write-Wins (LWW) silently overwrites concurrent updates based solely on timestamps. If machine clocks drift or events happen concurrently, valid human business decisions can be permanently destroyed.

quiz.question: Which system documents session consistency using session tokens?
options: Azure Cosmos DB
A bare HTTP connection
A DNS A record
quiz.explanation: Microsoft Azure Cosmos DB exposes session consistency as its default model, passing session tokens back and forth between client SDKs and replicas to enforce monotonic reads and read-your-writes.

quiz.question: Why is RPO different from a quorum size?
options: RPO specifies an acceptable data-loss window for a defined recovery scenario; quorum size specifies response requirements in a replication protocol
RPO always equals W
Quorum size measures API latency
quiz.explanation: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is a disaster recovery business metric measuring tolerated data loss duration (e.g. at most 5 seconds of writes). Quorum size (W) is a protocol setting specifying how many replicas must acknowledge a mutation.

scenarios.title: Why does the mathematical condition R + W > N NOT automatically guarantee Linearizability?
scenarios.context: An architect assumes that configuring N=3, R=2, W=2 in a leaderless datastore produces strong linearizability.
scenarios.answer: R + W > N guarantees that the read set and write set intersect on at least one replica. However, linearizability requires real-time global ordering: if client 1 finishes a write before client 2 begins a read, client 2 must see client 1's write. In leaderless quorum systems without consensus, a concurrent read can observe an in-progress write on 1 node, and a subsequent read by another client can hit 2 replicas that haven't received the write yet, causing time to appear to move backward! True linearizability requires consensus (Raft/Paxos) or synchronous read-repair write-back before responding.

scenarios.title: Why is Last-Write-Wins (LWW) considered dangerous for banking and grading, and how does CAS solve it?
scenarios.context: Apache Cassandra uses client-side timestamps to resolve concurrent writes by default.
scenarios.answer: LWW compares timestamps. If Instructor A grades an exam at 12:00:00.100 and Instructor B grades at 12:00:00.105 (due to clock skew), B's write silently overwrites A's write without warning. For financial ledgers or exam grades, Compare-and-Set (CAS) / Optimistic Concurrency Control must be used: `UPDATE grades SET score = 92, version = 2 WHERE id = 10 AND version = 1`. If version has advanced, the update aborts, forcing the application to handle the conflict explicitly.

scenarios.title: How do Session Tokens in Azure Cosmos DB implement Read-Your-Writes consistency efficiently?
scenarios.context: A user updates their avatar or password and refreshes their browser.
scenarios.answer: Cosmos DB passes a lightweight Session Token in the HTTP response header of every write. This token encodes the partition key and the Log Sequence Number (LSN) of the committed mutation. When the client makes subsequent reads, the SDK passes the session token to the replica. If the replica's local LSN is behind the token, the replica pauses until it catches up with the WAL stream before returning data, guaranteeing read-your-writes without routing all traffic to the primary.

scenarios.title: How does Google Cloud Spanner achieve external consistency without high-latency 2PC read locks?
scenarios.context: Executing distributed read-only queries across multiple geographical datacenters.
scenarios.answer: Spanner uses TrueTime (atomic clocks and GPS receivers) which exposes a bounded uncertainty window $\epsilon \le 7\text{ms}$. When a read-write transaction commits, Spanner waits out the uncertainty interval before releasing locks ('commit wait'). Because timestamps are strictly aligned with physical real-world time, read-only transactions can execute at a past timestamp without taking any database locks or communicating with Paxos leaders, guaranteeing linearizable historical snapshots with zero lock contention.

scenarios.title: Why does the Redis WAIT command NOT make Redis a strongly consistent database?
scenarios.context: An engineer executes `SET key val` followed by `WAIT 2 1000` to wait for 2 replica acknowledgements.
scenarios.answer: The official Redis documentation explicitly states that WAIT increases write durability confidence, but does not provide strong consistency. Redis replication is asynchronous. If a master crashes right after acknowledging a write to the client, but before replicas persist the write to disk (or if an asynchronous failover promotes an out-of-sync replica), the acknowledged write can be permanently lost. Redis lacks quorum consensus and synchronous multi-replica commit protocols.

scenarios.title: What is the difference between Read Repair and Anti-Entropy Repair in Cassandra?
scenarios.context: Maintaining consistency across replicas that drift apart due to network drops or node maintenance.
scenarios.answer: Read Repair is opportunistic and reactive: it only occurs when an application reads a key with a quorum level (e.g. QUORUM) and detects divergent versions between the queried replicas. If a key is written once and never read again, it will remain permanently out of sync. Anti-Entropy Repair (nodetool repair) is proactive: background processes build Merkle trees (cryptographic hash trees of partition ranges) and compare them between replicas to synchronize all drifted data.
